title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Jul 24, 2026
intro: This week's feed was dominated by Kimi K3 geopolitics; the real engineering signal came from teams publishing their eval gates, containment architectures, and context-management patterns.

cards.title: Gate agent releases on three-tier eval scores, not vibes
cards.problem: Motorway's dealer-search agent shipped with no way to catch tool-selection errors or multi-turn context drift before dealers saw them.
cards.apply: Score every candidate release on three thresholds — tool usage >95%, reasoning >85%, output quality >90% — using strands-agents-evals pre-deploy and Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations in production, and block deployment in a five-stage pipeline when any threshold misses. For non-deterministic runs, track pass^k (success across k consecutive trials) instead of a single pass/fail.
cards.result: Tool selection accuracy rose from 87% to 98%, task completion from 82% to 96%, and production incidents fell from 12/month to 2 — cutting incorrect results from 1 in 8 queries to 1 in 50.

evidence.note: AWS and Motorway report before/after production metrics for the pipeline.

cards.title: Treat agent context as a lifecycle to manage, not a log to truncate
cards.problem: Most production agent failures trace back to unmanaged context — bloated histories and tool definitions — not weak reasoning, and naive summarization trades accuracy for cost.
cards.apply: Split context management into five explicit stages: architecting the context structure, ingesting new information, scoping it to what's organizationally relevant, anticipating what will be needed next, and compacting/consolidating while preserving provenance of every kept fact.
cards.result: The reference implementation (Maximem Synap) hit 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo while achieving linear rather than quadratic cost growth as conversations lengthen.

evidence.note: Paper reports its own benchmark scores for the reference implementation.

cards.title: Offload multi-step logical reasoning to a Prolog MCP server, not the prompt
cards.problem: LLMs hallucinate systematically on multi-step logical reasoning once a compliance or safety rule base gets large, and semantic RAG can't enforce hard rules.
cards.apply: Expose a Prolog-backed MCP server (Euclid-MCP) that accepts a human-readable intermediate representation the LLM can generate directly, then run a translate-run-inspect-repair loop so the agent inspects proof traces and repairs its query instead of guessing at an answer.
cards.result: The paper reports that on an IT security/compliance benchmark, the LLM-only baseline held up on small rule sets but hallucinated on larger ones, while Euclid-MCP kept returning exact answers with lower latency and more compact output.

evidence.note: Paper reports a qualitative comparison on its own benchmark without exact percentages.

cards.title: Cut permission prompts by sandboxing the OS, not by asking more often
cards.problem: Per-action approval prompts stopped protecting anything once users were approving about 93% of them on reflex.
cards.apply: Replace prompt-based approval with OS-level sandboxes — Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux — that let the agent write inside its workspace but deny network access by default, and route any needed credentials through a proxy that only accepts a session-scoped token instead of raw secrets.
cards.result: Anthropic reports an 84% drop in permission prompts for Claude Code after the switch, with blast radius contained even when the agent processes untrusted input.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the measured drop in permission prompts after the sandbox change.

cards.title: Codify security review into CLAUDE.md and skills before code generation, not after
cards.problem: Manual security review can't scale once AI is authoring the majority of merged code — bugs need catching before they're generated, not after a human skims a diff.
cards.apply: Encode your org's security guidelines directly in CLAUDE.md and skills so generated code follows them from the first draft, run /security-review to flag attacker-controllable input during development, and stack multiple narrow-scope review agents (each with RAG context, none with full-repo authority) ahead of a human reviewer who samples risk-weighted approvals.
cards.result: Anthropic estimates about a third of past claude.ai incidents would now be caught automatically, and PR comment engagement rose from 16% to 54% as teams trusted the automated findings.

evidence.note: Anthropic reports the retrospective incident-catch estimate and comment-rate change.

cards.title: Normalize retrieved-fact salience before your multi-hop RAG agent reasons over it
cards.problem: A multi-hop RAG agent can be misled without a single false fact or injected instruction, just by reordering, emphasizing, or reframing truthful retrieved passages.
cards.apply: Add Salience Normalization as an input-side defense: flatten framing, emphasis, and positional cues on retrieved passages before they reach the reasoning step, so attribute binding across hops can't be redirected by presentation alone.
cards.result: Under a 30% edit budget, this 'salience induction' attack hit an 83.3% success rate across five model families; Salience Normalization cut that to 15.3% under standard attacks (23.6% against adaptive ones), while existing defenses left 75.7% of attacks succeeding.

evidence.note: Paper reports measured attack and defense success rates.

cards.title: Let the coding agent's own representations decide what context to prune
cards.problem: Context-pruning for coding agents usually means running a separate classifier over tool output — another model to host, tune, and keep in sync.
cards.apply: Attach a small head directly to the coding agent's own internal representations to emit a keep-or-prune label per line, using a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count, instead of standing up a separate pruning classifier.
cards.result: SWE-Pruner Pro cut prompt-plus-completion tokens by up to 39% while lifting SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8 points and long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points, with bounded inference overhead.

evidence.note: Paper reports measured token reduction and accuracy deltas.

cards.title: Have the agent write specs, and a deterministic kernel write the code
cards.problem: Agent-generated application code is hard to trust in production because there's no single artifact that's both the proof of correctness and the thing that actually runs.
cards.apply: Have the agent emit a formal specification — behavior as a state machine, data as machine-readable entity definitions, authorization as default-deny policy — and let a deterministic kernel verify it via symbolic reasoning, exhaustive state exploration, fault-injected simulation, and property testing before it becomes the running system.
cards.result: Datadog's Temper kernel makes agent output repeatable and inspectable because the verified specification is the deployed system, eliminating drift between what was proven safe and what ships.

evidence.note: The source describes the architecture qualitatively without a quantified production result.
